### Definition — Lesson — Least Fixed Point of the Relational Hyperverse

**Two fixed-point results, different in character.** The first-turn result §self-generation proved $R = U_G(R)$: every sheaf in $R$ is locally generated by representable objects. This is Grothendieck's density theorem — a within-level closure result.

The hyperverse fixed-point theorem proves $\mathcal{H} = U_\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{H})$: the entire hyperverse tower closes on itself at its colimit. This is a between-level fixed point — the closure operator is applied across universes, not within one. The mathematics is substantively different: where the density theorem follows from standard topos theory, the hyperverse fixed point requires the BC coherence of the tower (§beck-chevalley-tower) to justify exchanging the sheaf construction with the filtered colimit.

**The minimality half.** The theorem has two parts. The first part — $U_\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{H}) \cong \mathcal{H}$ — establishes that $\mathcal{H}$ is *a* fixed point. The second part establishes that it is the *least* fixed point: any proper sub-object of $\mathcal{H}$ that is closed under $U_\mathcal{H}$ must contain all of $\mathcal{H}$, which is a contradiction. The minimality is what makes $\mathcal{H}$ canonical — not just one self-universal structure, but the one with no redundancy.

**Why this is the payoff.** The fiber structure $(H_t, \sigma_t, \Delta_t, H_t^*)$ was introduced in §fiber-doctrine as an axiom: the data at each history. It was not obvious why these particular algebras, this particular shape. The fixed-point theorem provides the retroactive answer: a universe that satisfies $U_\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{U}) \cong \mathbf{U}$ must have, as its internal fiber algebras at the meta-level, the fixed fibers $H^*$ with trivial nuclei ($\sigma = \Delta = \mathrm{id}$). The nuclear quartet structure is the unique shape preserved at the fixed point. The axiom was not arbitrary — it was the only choice consistent with self-universality.
